headline: Prompts as Infrastructure: A Cross-Platform Library for Agentic Coders
lede: A curated prompt library for AI coding agents sounds modest until you understand the distribution mechanic. Jeffrey Emanuel's jeffreysprompts.com is built on the Agent Skills open standard—a format originally developed by Anthropic and since adopted by 35-plus tools—meaning a single SKILL.md file installs identically across Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex CLI, Google's Gemini CLI, and Cursor. Emanuel built the site in a single day and published the complete Claude Code session as proof of what the prompts can do.
body:
Emanuel, a former quant investor who now orchestrates dozens of AI coding agents simultaneously, built the site in a single day using Claude Code—publishing the entire session transcript as evidence. The premise is that useful prompts are infrastructure, not notes-to-self. jeffreysprompts.com lets users browse, copy, and export prompts organized by category, with a `jfp` CLI for terminal-first workflows and a **Pro tier** at $10 per month that adds cloud storage, personalized recommendations, and cost estimation.

The “install as skills” mechanic is the technically interesting piece. It builds on the *Agent Skills* open standard, originally developed by Anthropic, which defines a minimal format: a folder containing a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter and markdown instructions. Drop one into `~/.claude/skills/` and Claude Code registers it as a slash command; the same file works identically in OpenAI’s Codex CLI, Google’s (GOOGL) Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and more than 30 other tools that have adopted the standard—including JetBrains, ByteDance’s TRAE, Mistral AI, and Snowflake (SNOW). A prompt, in this model, is not a chat input but a portable, version-controlled capability.

The *progressive disclosure* design is worth noting: at startup, the agent loads only a skill’s name and a short description of 30 to 50 tokens; the full instructions enter the *context window* only when the skill is explicitly invoked—a sensible economy in a world where context is metered. Emanuel’s example prompts illustrate the format’s range: the Idea Wizard generates 30 candidate improvements, applies critical judgment to reject weak ones, and distills the survivors to five detailed plans complete with confidence scores; the Robot-Mode Maker helps developers design agent-optimized CLIs with structured JSON output.

The thread in which the bookmark appears touches a real tension in the field. The question of what makes an agentic release genuinely impressive—from a “systems and innovation level”—reflects a growing recognition that standard coding benchmarks do not capture real-world agent performance. Academic research supports the concern: FeatureBench, a 2025 paper evaluating agents on 200 complex feature-development tasks drawn from 24 real GitHub repositories, found that Claude 4.5 Opus—which scores 74.4% on *SWE-bench*, the dominant leaderboard—achieved only 11.0% on FeatureBench tasks, a gap of more than 60 percentage points. Benchmark selection shapes what gets optimized; the absence of honest benchmarks for agentic developer experience is precisely the gap Emanuel’s co-conversationalist @jp_aidev was groping toward.

Emanuel’s site enters a nascent but competitive market. Third-party platforms like SkillsMP have emerged around the same Agent Skills standard, and community repositories now host more than a thousand contributed SKILL.md files. His bet is on curation over volume—and on the proposition that a practitioner who maintains dozens of simultaneous AI agent subscriptions is himself evidence for what the prompts unlock. Whether that proves a durable competitive moat or merely a strong launch story depends on how quickly the Pro features ship.

concepts.definition: An open standard, originally developed by Anthropic, for packaging AI instructions as a reusable SKILL.md file with YAML metadata and a markdown body. Adopted by 35-plus AI coding tools as of 2026, so a skill written once works across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and many others.

The file at the heart of the Agent Skills standard: a single markdown document with YAML frontmatter declaring name, version, and tags, followed by natural-language instructions for the AI agent. Placed in the right directory, it becomes a slash command the agent can invoke on demand.

A block of structured metadata at the top of a text file, wrapped in triple dashes (---). Used in SKILL.md files to declare machine-readable fields like name and version without disrupting the human-readable markdown body below.

A loading strategy where only a minimal summary enters memory at startup; the full content loads on demand. Applied to AI agent skills, only the skill’s name and description occupy the context window by default, with complete instructions fetching only when the skill is explicitly called.

The maximum amount of text an AI model can hold in active memory at once, measured in tokens. Because larger contexts cost more compute and slow responses, managing what enters the context window is a practical concern in agentic workflows.

A widely used benchmark that tests AI coding agents on real GitHub issues: the agent must write a patch that makes existing failing tests pass. Criticized for not representing the complexity of feature development from scratch, and for correlating poorly with real-world agent performance on harder tasks.

Developer Experience (DX) applied to AI agent workflows—the quality of the conditions, including task clarity, prompt design, and feedback loops, under which an AI agent operates. Distinct from benchmarking the model itself; it evaluates the environment and tooling the developer provides.

repos.summary: The open-source codebase behind jeffreysprompts.com, written primarily in TypeScript. It includes the jfp CLI tool for browsing, searching, copying, and exporting prompts from the terminal, with an MCP server mode for agent-native use. The repo also hosts the SKILL.md files themselves, making the prompt library forkable and version-controlled.

thread_summary: @jp_aidev described their approach to evaluating agentic developer experience: asking teams what would make them super proud of a release from a systems and innovation perspective, and field-testing directly with AI agents. They mentioned developing an informal benchmark for agentic DX but not having time to productize it. @doodlestein’s reply pointed to jeffreysprompts.com as a related resource, noting the site is not yet officially launched.
